summary: No sourced study of a world without the 26th Amendment exists. 1972 data show 18–20s turned out about 2–3 points below 21–24s (48.3% vs 50.7%) and split roughly evenly between McGovern and Nixon, so removing them would likely have changed little. The 1970 statute might still have allowed them to vote for president.

notes:
**Caveat first.** The sources I found don't split vote choice or turnout by sex, nativity, race, or region for 18–20-year-olds. I found no reliable evidence on the groups your simulation distinguishes. I also found no scholarship on a world where the amendment failed. One point matters for the scenario: the 1970 Voting Rights Act amendment had already set 18 for federal elections. That amendment lowered the voting age in national elections to 18 in all states after January 1, 1971. [S2] The Supreme Court limited it. Under that ruling, 18- to 20-year-olds could vote for president and vice president but not for state officials. [S18] So the amendment's absence would not by itself bar 18–20s from voting for president in 1972. They would be barred only if the statute also failed. The scenario should say which.

## 1. Direct evidence (the 1972 electorate)

**Size of the group.** About 11 million new age-eligible voters would be 18 to 20, and about 14 million would be 21 to 24. [S2] Together, those under 25 made up 18 percent of the voting-age population. [S2]

**Turnout, 18–20 versus 21–24.**
- The EAC compilation of Census data gives, for 1972, 18–20-year-olds a 58.1% registration rate and 48.3% turnout. The 21–24 group had 59.5% registered and 50.7% turnout. [S3] That is a gap of about 2.4 percentage points.
- A teaching slide using similar data gives 48 for 18–20 and 51 for 21–24 [S5], a gap of about 3 points.
- Other sources round it differently. One has 52 percent of 18-to-24-year-olds voting against 68 percent of those 25 and older. [S8] A CIRCLE fact sheet that counts citizens only puts 18–24 turnout at 55% against 70% for those 25 and over [S9].
- Overall turnout was 55.6 percent of eligible voters [S6].

**Vote split.**
- Polls showed that student voters split about evenly between McGovern and Nixon. [S6]
- Wikipedia-sourced figures say Nixon took 48 percent of 18–24-year-olds and 52 percent of those under 30 [S7]. A separate Wikipedia passage says McGovern won 18–24s 52–46 [S10]. These two are inconsistent, and I haven't checked either against the underlying polls.
- Nixon's campaign found that non-college youth leaned toward Nixon and outnumbered college youth. [S7]
- I found no 18–20 versus older-first-time-voter split. That figure needs the Gallup or CBS/NES crosstabs, which I didn't locate.

**Effect on the outcome.** Nixon won in a landslide with 60.7% of the popular vote. [S10] Taking the 48/52 split as given, removing 18–20s would not plausibly have changed the winner. That is my inference, not a sourced finding. The McGovern campaign had predicted 18 million young voters, but exit polls indicate about 12 million. [S10]

## 2. Analogues (pre-1972 state experience)

- **Georgia (1943) and Kentucky (1955).** In states that allowed 18–20-year-olds to vote before the amendment, their voting rate was lower than that of 21–24-year-olds. [S19] That is the same direction as the 1972 national gap.
- **Kentucky 1956.** A University of Kentucky survey found some evidence of high initial participation by 18–21s. Enthusiasm was reported fading after the large initial vote in the 1956 presidential election. [S16] The survey also found most young voters split their tickets rather than following party registration [S16]. That was a small student sample.
- **Alaska and Hawaii.** They set the age at 19 and 20 when they became states in 1959. [S11] I found no turnout figures for them.
- **Group detail.** The Census report on new voters has 1968 tables for ages 18–24 by race, region and sex. One table covers participation and registration by race, residence, and region for November 1968. [S2] I only saw the table titles, not the numbers. That is the best lead for your group breakdown.

## 3. Named people

- **Richard Nixon.** He believed that only a constitutional amendment could lower the voting age. [S8] He signed the Voting Rights Act extension, expressing misgivings about its constitutionality. [S13] On election night in 1972 he said he had won a majority of young Americans' votes. [S6]
- **George McGovern.** He aimed much of his campaign at young voters, especially students, and was disappointed by the turnout. [S6]
- **Dwight Eisenhower.** In his 1954 State of the Union he urged Congress to propose a constitutional amendment allowing voting at 18. [S15]
- **Ellis Arnall.** As Georgia's young governor, he drove the 1943 reform. [S15]
- **Jennings Randolph.** He introduced the amendment 11 times between 1942 and 1971. [S4]

## 4. Limits

- **Survey measurement.** Turnout figures come from self-reported Census surveys. They differ by method, as the 55%, 52% and 50% versions above show.
- **Georgia and Kentucky.** They were small, mostly Southern, and in 1943 and 1955 were not presidential-campaign-driven settings. Georgia's reform came from no organized lobbying group [S15]. The 1972 electorate was nationwide, post-Vietnam, and had a different draft context.
- **Age ranges.** The 1972 vote splits mix 18–24 and under-30 groupings. They can't be read as 18–20 results.
- **Overlap with older cohorts.** The 21–24 group had also been newly eligible in many states, so it isn't a clean "experienced voter" comparison.
- **Group effects.** Any effects by sex, race, nativity or region would be extrapolations. I found nothing sourced on them.
prompt:
Scenario for the 1972 United States presidential election (election day 1972-11-07).
A reader asked: "Eighteen-to-twenty-year-olds cannot vote in 1972.".
As modelled: The 26th Amendment is never ratified, so citizens aged 18 to 20 cannot vote for president in 1972.
Kind of change: franchise. Populations it reaches first: every voter.
Include how newly enfranchised or newly barred groups actually turned out and voted the first times the rules changed for them.

Questions to answer:
- How did voters aged 18 to 20 split between the two major candidates in 1972 compared with older first-time voters?
- What was the turnout of 18-to-20-year-olds in 1972 relative to those aged 21 to 24?
- In states that already allowed voting before 21, such as Georgia and Kentucky, how did young voters behave in earlier elections?

Groups the simulation distinguishes: men and women; US-born non-Hispanic white, naturalized citizens of any race, noncitizens, US-born Black, and US-born Hispanic, Asian, American Indian and other adults; the Northeast, Midwest, South (the eleven former Confederate states), border states and West. Evidence by these groups is most useful.
